sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025 [D5][D206], a 7.3% CAGR.
The path was a step change, not a compounder: revenue grew 1.4% in FY2021, then 22.9% in FY2023 and 12.3% in FY2024 [D129][D179][D202].
The FY2023 jump came from higher rates lifting net interest income, which rose 33.8% that year [D174], with deposit margin expansion on higher rates cited across segments [P36][P37].
FY2025 growth slowed to 2.8% [D226] as net interest income rose 3.1% [D221], driven by Markets and Card balances but largely offset by deposit margin compression and lower rates [P28].
The window reads as a rate-cycle bank: the FY2022-FY2024 surge was largely a repricing windfall, and the FY2025 flattening suggests that tailwind has largely run.
North America remains the core at 76.6% of revenue in FY2025 [D249], but contributed only 0.2pp of growth that year [D251].
International carried the year: EMEA contributed 1.2pp [D276] and Asia-Pacific 1.2pp [D301], on 9.5% and 17.3% growth [D275][D300].
Net interest income was 52.3% of revenue in FY2025 [D209], up from 47.7% in FY2016 [D8], so the mix has shifted toward spread income.
Noninterest income grew only 2.4% in FY2025 [D222], as higher Markets and asset management fees were largely offset by the absence of the prior year's $7.9 billion Visa gain [P27].
EPS diluted grew 13.9% a year against net income's 9.7% [F115][F113], the gap coming from a 3.4% share-count reduction in FY2025 [D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025 [D207], better than the 57.2% window median [D333] and near the 51.7% window low of FY2024 [D331].
That is well below the banks peer median of 61.7% [D337], ranking at the 0th percentile [D336].
Noninterest expense rose 4.2% in FY2025 [D225], driven by higher compensation, brokerage and technology spend, partly offset by FDIC assessment releases [P26].
The credit-loss provision was 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 [D208], above the 6.0% peer median [D341] and the 5.6% FY2016 level [D7].
Net margin was 31.2% in FY2025 [D210] against a 21.4% effective tax rate [D203], so below-the-line items did not distort the operating picture.
Operating cash flow was negative $148 billion in FY2025 [F60], or -2.59x net income [D204], against $78.1 billion in FY2021 [F56].
The outflow came from higher trading assets, securities borrowed and loan originations, partly offset by net income [P21].
For a bank, operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure; the swings track trading and lending balance-sheet activity rather than profitability.
Capital return is the better lens: buybacks plus dividends of $48.2 billion in FY2025 [D205] against $57.0 billion of net income [F30].
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025 [D213], double the 11.8% banks peer median [D339] and at the 100th percentile [D338].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits in FY2025 [D211], up from 43.1% in FY2021 [D115] as lending grew into the deposit surge.
Loans rose $121.1 billion, driven by CIB Markets and AWM securities-based lending on higher client demand [P4].
Buybacks of $31.6 billion [X102] and dividends of $16.6 billion [X112] in FY2025 cut the diluted share count 3.4% [D224], lifting EPS growth above net income growth.
Net income for FY2021-FY2025 in the table comes from the proxy's pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, differing by up to 0.10% [R1][F30][X20].
The provision rose to $14.2 billion in FY2025 [X147] from $10.7 billion in FY2024 [X146], with criticized wholesale exposure up to $48.5 billion [P2].
The increase was driven by downgrades and new commitments in SPEs, Consumer & Retail and Banks & Finance Companies [P2].
Credit costs are rising from a low base and rank above the peer median, but the allowance at 1.8% of loans [D212] still looks adequate.
Watch the efficiency ratio: a move back above the 57.2% window median [D333] would reverse the FY2024-FY2025 cost discipline, visible in the FY2026 10-K.
Watch the credit-loss provision as a share of revenue: a rise above the FY2025 level of 7.8% [D208] would confirm the deteriorating criticized-exposure trend [P2].
Watch net interest income growth: a return above the FY2023 rate of 33.8% [D174] would signal the rate tailwind has resumed, while a fall below the FY2025 3.1% [D221] would confirm the flattening.
